children: (Latin) Such and so great is the depravity of our generation, O Citizens, that our materfamiliases greatly prefer the lascivious titillations of any barbaric half-man whomsoever to the ponderous testicles and extraordinary erections of Roman centurions.[1] Needless to say, this is not a quotation from the Classics, though the style is deliberately Ciceronian.

Mulligan’s libici is problematic. Thornton translates it as lustful, which would actually be libidinosi. Gifford translates it as Gallic, an allusion to the Libici, a Gallic people;[2] but Libicorum would be the correct form. In the first draft Joyce wrote Libycci (or Libyeci), so his original intention seems clear: Libyci (Libyan, African).[3]

The point of the passage is that Roman matrons prefer sexual satisfaction to conception: copulation without population, another form of contraception, which is the interpretation Joyce puts on the slaughter of the Oxen of the Sun in this episode.

children: While impersonating Burke, Joyce can’t resist an allusion to Shakespeare here. In Act V, Scene VI of
Henry VI
, Gloucester, who would soon become Richard III, stabs the protagonist, who has just compared himself to Daedalus, and his son to Icarus, and exclaims:
“I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear.
Indeed, ‘tis true that Henry told me of;
For I have often heard my mother say
I came into the world with my legs forward.”

Gloucester/Richard, we know, was born with a “crookback” deformity, and Joyce’s addition of “gibbosity,” which also means “hunchbacked”, further establishes the mention, whose purpose here is not only to echo “Burke’s” denouncing Irish youth as having “neither pity, love, nor fear,” but is also to point us to the
Ulysses
-specific reference to Daedalus and Icarus. The key to this reference occurs in the “"Scylla and Charybdis”
episode as Stephen is expounding his Shakespeare/Hamlet theory. Stephen is brought to remember the final entry in his diary in
A Portrait*:

“Fabulous artificer. The hawklike man. You flew. Whereto? Newhaven-Dieppe,steerage passenger. Paris and back. Lapwing. Icarus. Pater, ait. Seabedabbled, fallen, weltering.Lapwing you are. Lapwing be.”
What is the significance of “lapwing”? George L. Geckle, in his Winter 1969 article in the
James Joyce Quarterly
, takes us to an unsurprising third level of depth in answering it; William M. Schutte, quoting from Blake’s
Gnomic Verses

, describes a lapwing and then observes, “Blake’s lapwing, flying around on the barren heath instead of where the corn grows, ignorant both of where the soil is fruitful… , is a good symbol for the ambitious but often misdirected young man to whom Stephen refers… , a young man that could fly by all the nets that sought to restrain him.” Geckle argues that, while some critics may argue that Joyce would have been aware of the implications of these references, Stephen would not. He writes, “The Stephen in Ulysses, I would argue, becomes well aware of the implications of his references, especially when such references show the irony of his past aspirations and present failures. The ‘lapwing’ passage is proof that such is the case.”

children: Haines had experienced a nightmare in which appeared a black panther, whose terror he tried to end by shooting [destroying] it. Samuel Chenevix Trench, on whom Haines’s character is modeled, actually shot off a round from a revolver in experiencing the dream. The black panther, or leopard, is used several times in Biblical imagery.
Jeremiah 5:6

, for instance: “…a leopard shall watch over their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces: because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.“ The “leopard” doing the watching is a Christ figure, the choice of “cities,” here Dublin, whose “transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.” The black panther is also, in Slovenian folklore a symbol for Deep understanding and spirituality.
In
Gracious Wild: A Shamanic Journey with Hawks

, Stacey L. L. Couch tells us the black panther is a symbol of darkness, not just because of the color, but also because, “Jungles are wet, messy, jumbled places and they mirror the unkept [sic] and unknown part of our unconscious. Black panther spirit animal is adept at navigating the unconscious, hidden parts of ourselves. She ventures into the unknown, comfortable with the darkness. Black panther spirit animal understands that the jungle is fraught with danger and rich with resources. The shadow is both good and bad.” She also delves into many themes from Ulysses as she asserts that, “Black panther symbolism is not only about traveling into our own darkness, but also the mystery of the universe. Both jaguars and leopards are solitary animals, and black panther spirit animal lends us the courage to venture into the unknown alone.  The mystery of the universe is … the darkness of the womb, the place of pure potential creation… The void is a place beyond the five senses where we must venture on faith alone. The absence of moonlight makes black panther less visible and a superior huntress. The new moon is a time of both death and rebirth, when we stand at the threshold looking back at what was and looking ahead at what’s come. Neither are certain for this brief window in time. What was is no more and what’s to be is not yet born… The moon is strongly associated with the feminine as is the jungle and darkness, thus the black panther is said to carry the energy of the feminine principles of receptivity and intuition. Now is not the time for figuring things out or striking out, but for both turning inward to your soul and opening up to the Divine.”
The quote in the
Oxen of the Sun

episode complicates things further: “The black panther himself was the ghost of his own father.” Previous passages in which the phrase appears had clear references to Hamlet, and to Christ, whose father was referred to, sometimes indelicately, as the Holy Ghost. In Telemachus, however. Stephen hears his father’s voice as his own, for, as Mulligan has said, “he himself is the ghost of his own father.” This could infer that Stephen is either seen as another Irish victim, or, likelier (especially coming from Mulligan), a co-conspirator in Ireland’s destruction.

children: In
Oxen of the Sun

, Joyce has another objective in addition to just parodying Horace Walpole; he also adds commentary on the state of affairs in Ireland. He appoints Buck Mulligan spokesman, and has him relate, in his typically caustic and flippant manner, a tale that “began to freeze them with horror.” As R. M. Adams reminds us, “Ireland is a land of walking ghosts and barely vitalized corpses,” and Mulligan presents his listeners, in an ante room in the National Maternity Hospital, a highly unique staging for a mostly rowdy conversation among mostly young men, only some of whom, as medical students and residents, have a clear reason for being there. “The secret panel beside the chimney slid back and in the recess appeared… Haines!”

This highly symbolic character, and roommate to Mulligan and Stephen, is used at times in Ulysses to caricaturize the upper-crust, superior, dominating English who have “usurped” Ireland for their own exploitation. That, of the three roommates in the Martello tower, he, the Englishman, was the only one to have studied the “Erse” (Gaelic) language indicts the Irish as having abandoned its culture, and Haines is all too willing to laud it over the others for his eminence. Haines claims responsibility for the Childs murder case, in which the victim and his family, despite the victim’s brother being accused of the crime, were respectable, upper-middle class, the father a former service provider to the Viceroy, the victim a literary and highly respected Church of Ireland clergyman, whose open book on the history of the Bible was splattered with blood at the scene, the accused a successful accountant.

Could Joyce be inferring that Haines, as surrogate for the English, had destroyed this respectable, genteel part of Ireland, and left it with the crudeness and boorishness such as was displayed by this band of young men that evening at the hospital, educated, and seemingly accomplished as they were? The guilt-ridden ghost Haines exclaims, “My hell, and Ireland’s, is in this life. It is what I tried to obliterate my crime. Distractions, rookshooting…, laudanum…, In vain! His [Ireland’s?] spectre stalks me. Dope is my only hope… Ah! Destruction! The black panther!”

children: Griselda Steevens (1653 – 18 March 1746) was left an large income by her twin brother. A clause in Dr Steevens' will stipulated that on Griselda’s death, the income was to be used to provide a hospital for the poor of Dublin. Although the terms of Dr Steevens' will were that work on the hospital would not begin until after Griselda Steevens' death, she decided to begin work on the hospital in 1720. As a youth Griselda had suffered a disorder of the eyes, and since then had worn a veil while in sunlight. Shy and reclusive, while conducting her charitable works in the Dublin slums she would remain in her carriage while servants gave out alms to the poor. By 1723 a sufficient portion of the new Dr Steevens' Hospital was completed to accommodate 40 patients, in addition to Griselda’s apartments. Griselda lived in the hospital from 1723 until her death.

At some point, it became a common belief in Dublin that Griselda Steevens had a pig’s face. It is unclear when the rumour arose. Robert Chambers and Irish Georgian Society founder Desmond Guinness claim that the rumour was current in her lifetime, but Thomas Kirkpatrick, author of History of Dr Steevens' Hospital Dublin, says that “There is absolutely no evidence of this story in contemporary records, nor indeed does it appear to have been connected with the good lady until the nineteenth century”
